::: {.why}
A signal whose top and bottom deciles differ but whose middle is unordered is telling you something specific about where its information lives, and averaging it into one IC hides that.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Report quantile forward returns with intervals and test whether the ordering is monotone.
- Say what a non-monotone pattern with a strong extreme spread implies about the signal and about its capacity.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Build the quantile analysis in qlib/signals/evaluate.py: forward return per quantile with a standard error, the top-minus-bottom spread with an interval, and a formal test of monotonicity across quantiles rather than an eyeball judgement. Run it for all four signals at their chosen horizons.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Interpret the shapes you get: a signal that works only in the extremes has lower capacity than its IC suggests, because the tradeable names are fewer. Compute, for each signal, the fraction of the spread that comes from the extreme decile alone, and note which signals are concentrated that way.
:::
:::
